column1: Why does the visual cortex's hierarchical pipeline (retina → LGN → V1 → V2/V4 → IT) impose structural constraints on interface design?
column2: Because edge/contrast detection and object recognition happen through parallel pattern-matching in ~50ms, interfaces that violate spatial relationships or require serial scanning instead of parallel pattern recognition force costly, slower conscious processing.

column1: Why do low-contrast interfaces (e.g., light gray text on white) degrade usability at a neurological level?
column2: Retinal ganglion cells encode relative contrast differences, not absolute luminance; insufficient contrast imposes a preprocessing penalty before semantic processing can even begin.

column1: Define the Gulf of Execution and state what interface property it is a function of.
column2: The gap between a user's intention and the actions the system makes available to achieve it; it is a function of discoverability.

column1: Define the Gulf of Evaluation and state what interface property it is a function of.
column2: The gap between a system's output/state after an action and the user's ability to understand what actually happened; it is a function of feedback fidelity.

column1: What is the distinction between a 'perceived affordance' and an 'actual affordance' (Norman vs. Gibson)?
column2: An actual affordance is what the system genuinely supports functionally; a perceived affordance is what the user believes the system supports based on visual/interactive cues—these can diverge, causing interaction errors.

column1: A deployment UI shows a disabled 'Deploy' button with no explanation of why. What class of design failure is this, per the Gulf framework?
column2: An information-hiding bug: the system knows the precondition failure (e.g., branch untagged, approval pending) but fails to communicate it, widening the Gulf of Execution.

column1: What is the 'principle of least effort' in information architecture, and what common UI pattern does it explain?
column2: Users consistently choose the path minimizing total cognitive/mechanical cost, even if suboptimal; it explains why search bars dominate over deep hierarchical navigation, since searching minimizes time-to-insight under cognitive load.

column1: What is 'information scent' in information foraging theory?
column2: The semantic signal emitted by a link, label, or menu item that users evaluate against their information goal to decide which navigation path to pursue; strong scent occurs when terminology and hierarchy align with user intent.

column1: Why does information architecture fundamentally behave as a graph problem rather than a strict hierarchy?
column2: Every artifact (resource, log, metric) has multiple valid semantic relationships (hierarchical, sequential, relational, temporal), so no single organizational scheme satisfies all access patterns—navigation must support multiple traversal paths.

column1: What problem do design tokens solve, and what software engineering principle do they mirror?
column2: They abstract hardcoded values (colors, spacing, typography) into semantic variables that propagate changes atomically across a codebase, eliminating visual drift; this mirrors the DRY principle applied to visual/DOM rendering.

column1: What does the WCAG POUR mnemonic stand for, and how do design systems enforce it architecturally?
column2: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust; design systems bake correct ARIA semantics, focus management, and keyboard navigation into component primitives as compile-time constraints rather than runtime afterthoughts.

column1: In UI rendering performance, what latency budgets correspond to 60 FPS and 120 FPS, and why do they matter architecturally?
column2: 16.67ms per frame for 60 FPS and 8.33ms per frame for 120 FPS; the entire event dispatch → layout → display list build → GPU submission pipeline must complete within this budget to maintain perceptually smooth interaction.
